final_proof:
Let the two real data sequences be \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) and \(b=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)\), and write
\[
\bar a=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n a_i,\qquad \bar b=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n b_i.
\]
Because \(\mathbf C\) is assumed to be a correlation matrix, the correlations occurring in it are defined. Thus, under the usual Pearson definition, both centered sequences have positive squared norm:
\[
S_a=\sum_{i=1}^n(a_i-\bar a)^2>0,\qquad S_b=\sum_{i=1}^n(b_i-\bar b)^2>0.
\]
(The same proof applies if covariance and standard deviation are normalized by \(1/n\) or \(1/(n-1)\), since those common factors cancel.) For two such sequences \(x\) and \(y\), their correlation is
\[
 r(x,y)=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2}\,\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\bar y)^2}}.
\]
Consequently, the correlation matrix of \(a\) and \(b\) is
\[
\mathbf C=\begin{pmatrix}r(a,a)&r(a,b)\\ r(b,a)&r(b,b)\end{pmatrix}.
\]
For every index \(i\), multiplication of real numbers is commutative, so
\[
(a_i-\bar a)(b_i-\bar b)=(b_i-\bar b)(a_i-\bar a).
\]
The numerator in \(r(a,b)\) therefore equals the numerator in \(r(b,a)\), and their denominators are also equal, because the two positive factors have merely been interchanged. Hence \(r(a,b)=r(b,a)\). The diagonal entries are unchanged by transposition, so this equality of the off-diagonal entries proves \(\mathbf C^{\mathsf T}=\mathbf C\); thus \(\mathbf C\) is symmetric.

Finally, applying the definition with a sequence correlated with itself gives
\[
r(a,a)=\frac{S_a}{\sqrt{S_a}\sqrt{S_a}}=1,\qquad r(b,b)=\frac{S_b}{\sqrt{S_b}\sqrt{S_b}}=1,
\]
since \(S_a,S_b>0\). Thus every entry on the main diagonal of \(\mathbf C\) equals \(1\), as claimed. If either sequence were constant, its centered squared norm would be zero and its Pearson correlation would be undefined; in that case an ordinary correlation matrix for the two sequences would not exist, so the hypothesis that \(\mathbf C\) is a correlation matrix necessarily excludes that degenerate case.
